title: Founder's bookshelf
note: The best ideas of four books, merged by theme, each credited to its author: Ready, Fire, Aim (Michael Masterson), The Effective Executive (Peter F. Drucker), The Ideal Team Player (Patrick Lencioni) and Scaling People (Claire Hughes Johnson). Paraphrased from reviews and summaries, never the books' text. Refresh yearly to add titles.

concepts.s: Launch an imperfect product to paying customers fast, then refine it from what they do.

x.b:
• Masterson: ready: just enough preparation to deliver; fire: sell before it's polished; aim: improve from real customer response.
  • Masterson: speed is a weapon: ship new products before rivals can copy or substitute.

• Set the launch date before it feels finished.
  • Treat first sales as the test; fix what buyers complain about, ignore what only you care about.

Trap: Reading it as "skip preparation." It cuts excess planning, not the minimum readiness to deliver.
Trap: Using it where a failed launch is costly or irreversible: regulated or safety-critical products.
Synthesis: Same instinct as the lean-startup minimum viable product; it works best where a launch is cheap to run and to undo.

cards.q: What do "fire" and "aim" mean in Masterson's rule?
cards.a: Fire: sell before the product is polished. Aim: refine it from real customer response.

cards.q: Does ready, fire, aim mean skipping preparation?
cards.a: No. It cuts excess planning, not the minimum readiness to deliver.

cards.q: Where is ready, fire, aim a poor fit?
cards.a: Where a failed launch is costly or hard to undo, such as regulated or safety-critical products.

concepts.s: Each revenue stage has one main problem and needs a different founder, so solve the current stage's problem, not the next one's.

x.b:
Masterson: rough bands as summaries give them (names vary: infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood):

  1. About $0 to $1M: get the first profitable sale. Skill: selling.
  2. About $1M to $10M: launch many profitable products fast.
  3. About $10M to $50M: build systems, structure, real middle management.
  4. About $50M+: sustain growth as the company matures (summaries disagree on details).

• Name your stage, then its one main problem.
  • Change your own role at each boundary.
  • Don't install later-stage systems before a reliable first sale.

Trap: Treating the dollar bands as precise; they are rough markers.
Synthesis: Fits fast-cash product businesses best. A venture-funded company can skip ahead on investor money, so use it as an order of problems, not a revenue rule.

cards.q: Main problem of Masterson's first stage?
cards.a: Getting the first profitable sale; the skill is selling.

cards.q: Main problem of stage two (roughly $1M to $10M)?
cards.a: Launching several profitable products quickly.

cards.q: What does stage three (roughly $10M to $50M) demand?
cards.a: Systems, structure and capable middle management.

cards.q: What must the founder change at each stage boundary?
cards.a: Their own role and leadership style.

concepts.n: Sell first, then build the system
concepts.s: Until one channel reliably makes profitable sales, selling is the job; add structure only as fast as growth demands.

x.b:
• Masterson: stage one is about selling. Find the Optimal Selling Strategy: the right product, price, channel and way of selling. Get first sales, then sharpen the offer from what worked. One summary puts about 80% of founder time on customer acquisition.
  • Hughes Johnson: write down goals, principles and an operating rhythm as complexity grows; some of it can wait until you have traction.

• Log which offer, price and channel produced each sale.
  • Cut product work no buyer asked for.
  • Add a process only when its absence is costing you now.
Trap: Building branding, infrastructure or org charts before the first repeatable sale.

cards.q: What is Masterson's Optimal Selling Strategy?
cards.a: The combination of product, price, channel and selling approach that works.

cards.q: Sales or selling proposition first?
cards.a: First sales, then refine the proposition from what worked.

cards.q: When should you add a process?
cards.a: When its absence is costing you now.

concepts.s: Past the first million, grow by launching many improved products fast, each owned by a champion.

x.b:
• Masterson: improve existing products rather than invent from scratch; test fast and accept quick failures.
  • Masterson: every idea needs a champion with belief, authority and experience. No champion, postpone it.

• Keep a pipeline of product tests, one named owner each.
  • Kill tests that don't sell, fast.
  • Start hiring the people who will run next stage's systems.
Synthesis: Stage two (speed, many launches) and stage three (systems, control) pull against each other; the founder's hard job is timing the switch.

cards.q: What should the stage-two company become?
cards.a: An idea factory launching many profitable products quickly.

cards.q: Invention or improvement in stage two?
cards.a: Improvement on existing products.

cards.q: What does an idea's champion need?
cards.a: Belief in it, authority to execute, experience to steer. No champion: postpone.

concepts.s: Measure your time as it's spent, cut and delegate the waste, and pool what's left into long blocks.

x.b:
1. Drucker: record time in real time for three to four weeks, about twice a year; memory misreports it.
  2. Manage: drop what produces nothing, delegate what others can do as well, stop wasting others' time.
  3. Consolidate: knowledge work needs long uninterrupted blocks; scattered minutes produce little.

• Run the log now; mark each block keep, delegate or drop.
  • Protect one long block a day before meetings refill it.
Trap: Reconstructing the week from memory. It flatters you.

cards.q: Drucker's three time steps?
cards.a: Record, manage (cut and delegate), consolidate into large blocks.

cards.q: How long and how often should the time log run?
cards.a: Three to four weeks, about twice a year.

cards.q: Why log in real time?
cards.a: Memory misreports how time was spent.

concepts.s: Judge your work by what it changes in results outside your own team, never by hours or activity.

x.b:
• Drucker: an executive is any knowledge worker whose decisions affect results, whatever the title.
  • Drucker: effectiveness is getting the right things done; efficiency is doing things right.
  • Drucker: contribute in three areas: direct results, values, and developing people for tomorrow.
  • Drucker: people grow to the demands they make on themselves.

• Write one line: what outside result changes if I do my job very well?
  • Check goals cover all three areas, not just this quarter's numbers.

cards.q: Drucker's definition of an executive?
cards.a: Any knowledge worker whose decisions materially affect results, whatever the title.

cards.q: Effectiveness vs efficiency?
cards.a: Effectiveness: the right things done. Efficiency: doing things right.

cards.q: Drucker's three areas of contribution?
cards.a: Direct results, values, and developing people for the future.

concepts.n: Concentrate: few goals, kill the rest
concepts.s: Pick very few priorities, repeat them constantly, and deliberately stop everything else.

x.b:
• Drucker: first things first, one at a time. Set posteriorities (what you stop or never start); that takes courage more than analysis.
  • Masterson: kill product tests that don't sell, fast.
  • Hughes Johnson: the goal framework matters less than few clear goals repeated again and again and reviewed publicly on one predictable cadence. Track input metrics your team controls, not only outputs.

• Keep a stop-doing list beside the to-do list.
  • Drop any project you wouldn't start today.
  • Review metrics weekly; hold strategy reviews on a separate calendar.

Trap: Prioritizing by adding: a ranked list with nothing removed just reorders the overload.
Trap: Frequent metrics reviews, rare strategy reviews: strategy shrinks to this week's numbers.

cards.q: What are posteriorities?
cards.a: Tasks you decide to stop or never start.

cards.q: What matters more than the goal framework, per Hughes Johnson?
cards.a: Few clear goals, communicated again and again.

cards.q: Why track input metrics?
cards.a: They lead results and the team controls them.

cards.q: Why does Drucker call priority-setting a matter of character?
cards.a: The analysis is easy; dropping things takes courage.

concepts.n: Decide once, then write the rule
concepts.s: Decide recurring problems once as written principles, and make one-off decisions by a clear process with dissent.

x.b:
1. Drucker: classify: generic problems get a rule; true exceptions are handled one at a time.
  2. Boundary conditions: the minimum the decision must achieve.
  3. What's right before what's acceptable, or you can't tell good compromises from bad.
  4. Build in action: who must know, who acts, with what resources.
  5. Feedback: test against what actually happens. Distrust decisions with no dissent.
  • Hughes Johnson: write a mission, long-term goals and principles that settle real trade-offs; each team writes a charter.

• The second time a question reaches you, write the rule.
  • Delete any principle that has never decided anything.
  • Ask for the strongest objection before deciding.

Trap: Patching a recurring problem case by case.
Trap: Values as slogans that settle no trade-off.

cards.q: Drucker's first question about any problem?
cards.a: Generic or exceptional? Generic gets a rule.

cards.q: Why decide what is right before what is acceptable?
cards.a: Otherwise you can't tell a good compromise from a bad one.

cards.q: How did Drucker view a decision with no disagreement?
cards.a: With suspicion: nobody examined the alternatives.

cards.q: Hughes Johnson's founding documents?
cards.a: Mission, long-term goals, principles; plus team charters.

concepts.s: Staff and work around what people do uncommonly well, and accept the weaknesses that come with it.

x.b:
• Drucker: make productive the strengths of your colleagues, your boss and yourself.
  • Drucker: absence of weakness is no qualification.
  • Drucker: manage up by helping your boss do what they do well, not by changing them.

• Name each report's standout strength; is their role built around it?
  • In hiring, ask "what will they do exceptionally well?" before "what are their gaps?"

Trap: Hiring the well-rounded candidate with no standout strength.
Trap: Using strength to excuse a weakness that blocks the job, such as integrity.

cards.q: Whose strengths should an executive make productive?
cards.a: Colleagues', the boss's and one's own.

cards.q: What should you staff for?
cards.a: What a person does uncommonly well.

cards.q: How does Drucker say to manage your boss?
cards.a: Help them do what they do well.

concepts.s: An ideal team player has all three: little ego, self-driven effort for the team, and sense about people.

x.b:
• Lencioni: humble (shares credit, team first; the most important), hungry (self-motivated, does what's needed), smart (people sense, not IQ).
  • Lencioni: two of three gives predictable failures:
    • Accidental mess-maker: humble and hungry, not smart.
    • Lovable slacker: humble and smart, not hungry.
    • Skillful politician: hungry and smart, not humble; the most dangerous because they fake humility.
  • Lencioni: one of three: pawn (humble), bulldozer (hungry), charmer (smart).

• Rate yourself and your team on all three; discuss in one-to-ones.
  • Coach one virtue at a time with observed behavior.
  • Use the same words in hiring, reviews and recognition.

Trap: Reading "smart" as intellect.
Trap: Labeling colleagues casually or using the model to rank or fire; it is a coaching language.
Synthesis: It screens team behavior, not job ability; pair it with a skills check.

cards.q: Lencioni's three virtues?
cards.a: Humble, hungry, smart.

cards.q: Which virtue matters most?
cards.a: Humble.

cards.q: Hungry and smart, not humble?
cards.a: The skillful politician: most dangerous, fakes humility.

cards.q: Humble and hungry, not smart?
cards.a: The accidental mess-maker.

cards.q: Humble and smart, not hungry?
cards.a: The lovable slacker.

concepts.s: Hire from a standing pipeline with honest job descriptions, scoring every candidate on one rubric for strength and humble, hungry, smart.

x.b:
• Hughes Johnson: build the pipeline before a seat opens; describe the real work, not a warm picture; one simple rubric for every interviewer.
  • Lencioni: interview as a team, debrief right after each interview on the three virtues, probe lingering doubts, check references against them, and tell candidates what you hire for so some self-select out.
  • Drucker: score the role's key strength first.

• Rubric: key strength, then humble, hungry, smart.
  • Ask about wins and listen for "we" over "I"; ask for the biggest failure in specifics.

Trap: Panic hiring when a seat opens; the bar drops.
Trap: Letting a strong résumé override a doubt on humility.
Synthesis: Unstructured interviews predict poorly in hiring research; a fixed rubric is where Hughes Johnson's process and Lencioni's criteria meet.

cards.q: Hughes Johnson's first step to hiring well?
cards.a: Build a recruiting pipeline.

cards.q: What to listen for when candidates describe wins?
cards.a: "We" more than "I".

cards.q: Why tell candidates you hire for the three virtues?
cards.a: Some who lack them self-select out.

cards.q: Job-description mistake to avoid?
cards.a: Selling a warm picture instead of stating the real work.

concepts.s: Write down how you work, share it, and give direct feedback built on observed examples.

x.b:
• Hughes Johnson: leadership starts with self-awareness: write a working with me guide (how you like to work; how you handle work emotionally), share it and ask what's wrong.
  • Hughes Johnson: say the thing you think you can't; observe someone across several situations before giving feedback.
  • Lencioni: "smart" (reading people) starts with reading yourself.

• Draft your guide in 30 minutes and share it.
  • Ask new hires to write theirs.
  • Bring two or three observed examples to any hard conversation.
Trap: Treating your guide as a rulebook others must adapt to; it starts a mutual adjustment.

cards.q: Two parts of a working-with-me guide?
cards.a: How you like to work, and how you handle work emotionally.

cards.q: What should precede feedback?
cards.a: Observing performance across several situations.

cards.q: What does "say the thing you can't say" guard against?
cards.a: Over-filtering important feedback.
